title: JavaScript Essentials
description: Learn the core of JavaScript, from values and variables to functions and loops.

lessons.title: Values and types
lessons.goal: Tell numbers, strings and booleans apart, and print a value or its type with console.log.

slides.html:
LESSON 1 | IDEA

Values and types

A value is one piece of information a program works with.

42
number
"hello"
string
true
boolean
slides.narration: Every program works with values. A value is one piece of information, like a count, a word, or a yes or no answer. JavaScript sorts values into types. In this lesson you will meet three of them and learn how to ask JavaScript which type a value has.

slides.html:
LESSON 1 | CONCEPT

Three types

number: 42 or 3.5
string: text inside quotes
boolean: true or false
console.log(42)
console.log("hello")
console.log(true)
Prints
42
hello
true
slides.narration: A number is something you can count or measure, like 42 or 3.5. A string is text, and it always sits inside quotes. A boolean is either true or false. The command console.log shows a value on the screen. Notice that the quotes around hello are not printed.

slides.html:
LESSON 1 | EXAMPLE

Ask for the type

console.log(typeof 42)
console.log(typeof "42")
console.log(typeof false)
Prints
number
string
boolean
Quotes make a string, even around digits.
slides.narration: To ask for a type, write typeof before a value. The number 42 gives number. But 42 inside quotes is text, so typeof says string. The quotes decide the type, not the characters inside. And true without quotes is a boolean.

slides.html:
LESSON 1 | RECAP

Remember

Every value has a type: number, string or boolean.
Quotes make a string.
typeof shows the type. console.log shows the value.
slides.narration: Remember two things. First, every value has a type, and quotes make a string, even around digits. Second, console.log shows a value, and typeof tells you its type. When you are unsure what you are holding, ask typeof.

test.prompt: Which of these values is a string?
test.explanation: A value in quotes is a string, even when it contains only digits. 7 and 7.5 are numbers and true is a boolean.

test.prompt:
What does this code print?

console.log(typeof "true")
test.explanation: typeof reports the type of the value after it. "true" is in quotes, so it is a string, not a boolean.

test.prompt:
What appears on the screen when this code runs?

console.log("Hi")
test.explanation: console.log shows the value itself, so the quotes that mark a string are not printed.

variants.prompt: A program contains these four values. Which one is text rather than a number or a boolean?
variants.explanation: The quotes turn "7" into text. The other values have no quotes, so they are numbers or a boolean.

variants.prompt: JavaScript reads one of these values as a string. Which one?
variants.explanation: Quotes make a string, so "7" is text even though it looks like a number.

variants.prompt:
Run this line in Node. What shows up on the screen?

console.log(typeof "false")
variants.explanation: The quotes make "false" a string, so typeof says string.

variants.prompt:
What is printed by this single line?

console.log(typeof "100")
variants.explanation: Digits inside quotes are text, so the type is string.

variants.prompt:
A learner runs this line. What does the screen show?

console.log('Hi')
variants.explanation: Single or double quotes both make a string, and neither is printed.

variants.prompt:
Which output does this line produce?

console.log("Hi");
variants.explanation: The semicolon changes nothing. console.log prints the string without its quotes.

lessons.title: let and const
lessons.goal: Create variables with let and const, reassign a let, and choose clear names.

slides.html:
LESSON 2 | IDEA

let and const

A variable is a name for a value, so you can use the value again.
slides.narration: Programs need to remember things, like your score in a game. A variable is a name attached to a value, a bit like a labelled box. Once a value has a name, you can use it again and again. Today you will learn two ways to create variables.

slides.html:
LESSON 2 | CONCEPT

Declare a variable

let score = 10
console.log(score)
Prints
10
Names start with a letter and have no spaces. Style: bestScore. Capitals matter.
slides.narration: Write let, then a name, then an equals sign, then the value. Now score holds 10, and console.log prints it. A name starts with a letter and has no spaces or dashes. The usual style joins words and capitalises each new one, like bestScore. Capitals matter, so score and Score are different names.

slides.html:
LESSON 2 | EXAMPLE

let changes, const stays

let lives = 3
lives = 2
const planet = "Earth"
console.log(lives)
console.log(planet)
Prints
2
Earth
let: can get a new value. const: cannot, or you get an error.
slides.narration: A let variable can be reassigned. Here lives starts at 3, then becomes 2, so the log prints 2. A const variable can never be reassigned, and trying to do it gives an error. A good habit is to start with const, and use let only when the value must change.

slides.html:
LESSON 2 | RECAP

Remember

let can be reassigned. const cannot.
Start with const. Use let only when the value must change.
Clear names: bestScore, not best score.
slides.narration: Remember two things. First, let makes a variable you can change later, and const makes one that stays fixed. Start with const when you are not sure. Second, choose clear names like bestScore, starting with a letter and without spaces.

test.prompt:
What does this code print?

let coins = 5
console.log(coins)
test.explanation: The variable coins holds the value 5, so console.log(coins) prints that value, not the name.

test.prompt: You write const age = 30 and later change it with age = 31. What happens?
test.explanation: A const cannot be reassigned, so JavaScript stops with an error. Only let allows a new value.

test.prompt: Which name is a good variable name for a player's best score, in the usual style?
test.explanation: Names cannot contain spaces or dashes or start with a digit. bestScore follows the usual style.

variants.prompt:
A tiny program stores a number and then shows it. What is printed?

let points = 5
console.log(points)
variants.explanation: points holds 5, so the value 5 is printed rather than the name.

variants.prompt:
Which output do these two lines produce?

let level = 5
console.log(level)
variants.explanation: Logging a variable shows the value stored in it, here 5.

variants.prompt: A program declares const age = 30 and then, a few lines later, runs age = 31. What is the result?
variants.explanation: const means the name cannot get a new value, so the second line causes an error.

variants.prompt: A variable was created with const age = 30. Later the code tries age = 31. Which statement is true?
variants.explanation: Reassigning a const fails with an error. It does not silently keep or change the value.

variants.prompt: You need a variable that holds the highest score a player reached. Which name is allowed and follows the usual style?
variants.explanation: Only bestScore-style names work. Spaces, dashes and a leading digit are not allowed.

variants.prompt: Pick the one name JavaScript accepts that also reads well.
variants.explanation: bestScore has no space or dash and starts with a letter, so it is valid.

lessons.title: Strings, numbers and comparisons
lessons.goal: Build text with template literals, avoid the plus trap, and compare values with ===.

slides.html:
LESSON 3 | IDEA

Strings, numbers and comparisons

console.log("5" + 3)
console.log("5" - 3)
Prints
53
2

Same pieces, different result. Why?
slides.narration: Look at these two lines. Both use the string 5 and the number 3, but one prints 53 and the other prints 2. When a plus sign has text next to it, it joins the pieces together. Minus can only do maths, so it works on the numbers. Keep this in mind for the rest of the lesson.

slides.html:
LESSON 3 | CONCEPT

Build text

const name = "Mia"
const stars = 2 * 3
console.log("Hello, " + name + "!")
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`)
console.log(`${name} has ${stars} stars`)
Prints
Hello, Mia!
Hello, Mia!
Mia has 6 stars
slides.narration: There are two ways to build text from values. You can join pieces with plus. Or you can use backticks and put each value inside a dollar sign and curly braces, which is a template literal. It is easier to read. Maths works as usual, and the asterisk means times.

slides.html:
LESSON 3 | EXAMPLE

Compare values

console.log(5 === 5)
console.log(5 === "5")
console.log(7 > 3)
console.log(7 >= 7)
Prints
true
false
true
true
=== checks value and type. Use it by default. There is also ==, which is looser: avoid it.
slides.narration: To compare values, JavaScript gives you true or false. Three equals signs check that the value and the type are the same, so 5 equals 5 is true but 5 and the string 5 are not equal. The signs greater than and greater than or equal compare sizes. Use three equals signs as your default.

slides.html:
LESSON 3 | RECAP

Remember

A plus next to a string joins text. Minus always does maths.
Backticks and a dollar sign with braces build text clearly.
Compare with ===, which also checks the type.
slides.narration: Remember two things. A plus next to text joins, while minus does maths, and template literals build text more cleanly. And when you compare, reach for three equals signs, because it also checks the type.

test.prompt:
What does this code print?

const pet = "cat"
console.log(`I have a ${pet}`)
test.explanation: Inside backticks, ${pet} is replaced by the value of pet, so the sentence ends with cat.

test.prompt:
What shows on the screen?

console.log("4" + 2)
test.explanation: A plus with a string next to it joins text, so "4" and 2 become 42. It is not added as numbers.

test.prompt:
What does this line print?

console.log(10 === "10")
test.explanation: === checks the type as well as the value. 10 is a number and "10" is a string, so the answer is false.

variants.prompt:
A learner builds a sentence with a template literal. What is shown?

const animal = "cat"
console.log(`I have a ${animal}`)
variants.explanation: ${animal} is replaced by the stored value, cat.

variants.prompt:
This version joins pieces with plus instead. What is printed?

const word = "cat"
console.log("I have a " + word)
variants.explanation: Plus joins the text and the value, giving the same sentence.

variants.prompt:
Both pieces here are strings. What does the program print?

console.log("4" + "2")
variants.explanation: Plus joins two strings end to end, giving 42.

variants.prompt:
A beginner expects 6. What does this line really print?

console.log('4' + 2)
variants.explanation: With a string present, plus joins instead of adding, so the result is 42.

variants.prompt:
What is the result of this comparison?

console.log(3 === "3")
variants.explanation: A number and a string are different types, so === gives false.

variants.prompt:
Run this check. What appears?

console.log("7" === 7)
variants.explanation: The types differ (string and number), so === is false even though the digits match.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.goal: Write a function with a parameter, return a value from it, and write the same function as an arrow function.

slides.html:
LESSON 4 | IDEA

Functions

A function is a named recipe you write once and use many times.

in
parameter
steps
the body
out
return
slides.narration: Sometimes you repeat the same steps again and again. A function is a named recipe: you write the steps once, give them a name, and then use them whenever you need. It can also take ingredients in and hand a result back. Let us see how to write one.

slides.html:
LESSON 4 | CONCEPT

Write and call

function double(n) {
  return n * 2
}
console.log(double(4))
Prints
8
slides.narration: Write function, then a name, then the parameter in brackets. A parameter is a name for the value that goes in. The word return sends a result back out. To use the function, call it by writing its name with a value in brackets. Here double of 4 gives 8.

slides.html:
LESSON 4 | EXAMPLE

return or console.log

function square(n) {
  return n * n
}
const a = square(3)
const b = square(a)
console.log(a)
console.log(b)
Prints
9
81
No return line: the call gives back undefined.
slides.narration: Return hands a value back, so you can store it or pass it into another call. Here square of 3 is 9, and square of 9 is 81. A function that only prints with console.log gives nothing back. Its result is undefined, which means no value.

slides.html:
LESSON 4 | RECAP

A shorter form

const double = (n) => n * 2
console.log(double(4))
Prints
8
return gives a value back. console.log only shows it.
slides.narration: There is a shorter way to write a function, called an arrow function. It means the same thing as before. Remember two things. Use return to give a value back, and console.log only to look at a value. An arrow function is just a second way to write a function.

test.explanation: double(6) runs return n * 2 with n set to 6, which gives 12.

test.prompt: A function show(n) only prints n * 2 on the screen and has no return line. What does const x = show(4) store in x?
choices: Nothing useful, because no value was returned
test.explanation: Without return the call gives back undefined, so x holds no useful value. Printing and returning are different jobs.

test.prompt:
What does this code print?

const triple = (n) => n * 3
console.log(triple(5))
test.explanation: An arrow function is another way to write a function. triple(5) returns 5 * 3, which is 15.

variants.explanation: twice(6) returns 6 * 2, which is 12.
addTwo(10) returns 10 + 2, so 12 is printed.

variants.prompt: A function prints its result on the screen but never returns it. You write const y = f(4). What is y?
choices: Nothing useful, because no value was returned
variants.explanation: Printing does not hand a value back. Only return does, so y has no useful value.

variants.prompt: Which is true of a function whose only job is to print, with no return, when you store its call in a variable?
choices: Nothing useful, because no value was returned
variants.explanation: Nothing was returned, so the variable gets undefined, not the printed number.

variants.prompt:
Here is a function written in the arrow form. What does it print?

const times3 = (x) => x * 3
console.log(times3(5))
variants.explanation: times3(5) returns 5 * 3, which is 15.

variants.prompt:
What is the output of this arrow function call?

const plus10 = (n) => n + 10
console.log(plus10(5))
variants.explanation: plus10(5) returns 5 + 10, which is 15.

lessons.title: Conditionals
lessons.goal: Choose between paths with if, else if and else, and combine conditions with && and ||.

slides.html:
LESSON 5 | IDEA

Conditionals

A conditional runs different code depending on a true or false question.

if
true? run this
else
otherwise this
slides.narration: Programs make decisions. If it is raining, take an umbrella. Otherwise, leave it at home. A conditional lets your code choose a path based on a question with a true or false answer. You will learn if, else if and else, and how to combine questions.

slides.html:
LESSON 5 | CONCEPT

if and else

const age = 16
if (age >= 18) {
  console.log("adult")
} else {
  console.log("minor")
}
Prints
minor
slides.narration: Write if, then a condition in brackets, then the code to run inside curly braces. If the condition is true, that code runs. If it is false, the else code runs instead. Here age is 16, which is not 18 or more, so the program prints minor.

slides.html:
LESSON 5 | EXAMPLE

Chains and combos

const age = 20
const hasTicket = true
if (age >= 18 && hasTicket) {
  console.log("enter")
} else if (age >= 18) {
  console.log("buy a ticket")
} else {
  console.log("too young")
}
Prints
enter
slides.narration: Use else if to check more cases in order. The first condition that is true wins, and the rest are skipped. Two ampersands mean and, so both sides must be true. Here the person is 20 and has a ticket, so the first branch runs and prints enter.

slides.html:
LESSON 5 | RECAP

and, or

console.log(true && false)
console.log(true || false)
Prints
false
true
&& needs both true. || needs at least one true. First true branch wins.
slides.narration: Remember two things. In an else if chain, the first true condition wins. And for combining questions, and needs both sides true, while or needs at least one side true. True and false gives false, but true or false gives true.

test.explanation: temp is 30, and 30 > 25 is true, so the if branch runs. The else branch is skipped.
The score 85 is not 90 or more, so the first test fails. 85 >= 80 is true, so B prints and the chain stops.

test.prompt:
What does this code print?

const raining = true
const hasUmbrella = false
console.log(raining && hasUmbrella)
test.explanation: && needs both sides true. hasUmbrella is false, so the whole expression is false.

variants.explanation: 35 > 25 is true, so the if branch prints hot.
25 >= 25 is true, so the if branch runs and prints hot.
80 fails the first test but passes score >= 80, so B prints.
89 is below 90 but at least 80, so only the else if branch runs.

variants.prompt:
Two flags are combined with and. What is printed?

const sunny = false
const warm = true
console.log(sunny && warm)
variants.explanation: and needs both sides true, and sunny is false, so the result is false.

variants.prompt:
Here the or operator joins two false values. What is shown?

console.log(false || false)
variants.explanation: or needs at least one true side. Both are false, so the result is false.

lessons.title: Arrays and loops
lessons.goal: Store a list in an array, read items by index, and loop over them to compute a total.

slides.html:
LESSON 6 | IDEA

Arrays and loops

An array is an ordered list. Positions start at 0.
slides.narration: Real programs deal with many values at once, like a list of scores or names. An array holds a list of values in order. Then a loop lets you do something with every item without writing the same line again and again. We start with arrays.

slides.html:
LESSON 6 | CONCEPT

Arrays

const scores = [4, 8, 6]
console.log(scores[0])
console.log(scores.length)
scores.push(10)
console.log(scores.length)
Prints
4
3
4
slides.narration: An array is written with square brackets and commas. You read an item with its position, called the index, and counting starts at zero, so the first item is at index 0. The length tells you how many items there are, and push adds a new item to the end.

slides.html:
LESSON 6 | EXAMPLE

for...of

const names = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cy"]
for (const name of names) {
  console.log(name)
}
Prints
Ana
Ben
Cy
slides.narration: A for of loop visits each item in an array, one at a time. On each turn, the name before of holds the current item. Here name is Ana, then Ben, then Cy, and the body runs once for each. You write the body once, and it repeats for every item.

slides.html:
LESSON 6 | RECAP

Add them up

const scores = [4, 8, 6]
let total = 0
for (const score of scores) {
  total = total + score
}
console.log(total)
Prints
18
slides.narration: Loops are great for totals. Start a let variable at zero, then add each item to it inside the loop. After the loop ends, total holds the sum, here 4 plus 8 plus 6, which is 18. Remember: arrays start at index 0, and for of visits every item.

test.prompt:
What does this code print?

const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"]
console.log(colors[1])
test.explanation: Positions start at 0, so index 1 is the second item, green. Index 0 would be red.
The loop body runs once per item and prints each item times 2, so three lines appear: 2, 4 and 6.

test.prompt:
What does this code print?

const prices = [3, 5, 2]
let total = 0
for (const price of prices) {
  total = total + price
}
console.log(total)
test.explanation: total starts at 0 and each loop turn adds one price: 3 + 5 + 2 makes 10, printed once after the loop.

variants.prompt:
A list of lights is stored in an array. Which item does this line show?

const lights = ["red", "green", "amber"]
console.log(lights[1])
variants.explanation: Index 1 is the second item, because counting starts at 0.

variants.prompt:
Read the array carefully. What is printed?

const tray = ["blue", "red", "green"]
console.log(tray[2])
variants.explanation: Index 2 is the third item, which is green here.
Each item is doubled and printed on its own line: 2, 4, 6.
The body runs three times, printing 2, then 4, then 6.

variants.prompt:
A shopping basket is summed with a loop. What is printed at the end?

const bag = [4, 4, 2]
let total = 0
for (const item of bag) {
  total = total + item
}
console.log(total)
variants.explanation: 4 + 4 + 2 is 10, and it is printed once because console.log sits after the loop.

variants.prompt:
This loop adds up four numbers. What does it print?

const costs = [1, 2, 3, 4]
let sum = 0
for (const cost of costs) {
  sum = sum + cost
}
console.log(sum)
variants.explanation: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 is 10, printed once after the loop ends.
